Kinematically Aligned Knee Arthroplasty

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A groundbreaking new technique for knee replacement has been performed in an African-first surgery right here in Johannesburg, led by renowned surgeon Dr. Hannes Jonker.

Unique Selling Point:
You might assume that when replacing body parts with implants, they should be aligned in a straight line—specifically in alignment with the hip, knee, and ankle (HKA alignment, both from the front and the side). This approach, known as mechanical alignment, has been the traditional method for implanting knee replacement prostheses. The idea was that this alignment would reduce stress on the knee, promoting the long-term durability of the implant. However, our bodies aren’t perfectly designed; individuals often have anatomical variations in their knees and surrounding ligaments due to normal wear and tear.
Since 2019, the perspective on prosthesis implantation has shifted to a new philosophy called kinematic alignment, which has shown significantly better outcomes. This approach aligns the prosthetic with your body’s natural or native alignment—essentially reflecting how your body functioned when you were in your 20s and pre-arthritic. Kinematic alignment is a fresh perspective on implants and has been applied to other types of prosthetics, such as hip replacements. What is different in this ‘Africa first’ surgery is that it’s the first time an actual implant has been specifically designed and implemented (the SpheriKA prosthesis) around this innovative philosophy. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGuGJSxpLoE
“Kinematic Alignment (KA) is a technique designed to restore the knee to its pre-arthritic anatomical alignment. It focuses on customising replacement components to a patient’s unique anatomy, biomechanics and motion patterns, aiming to achieve more natural knee movement, better functional outcomes, improved range of motion and greater implant durability.”

The first surgery in Africa using this prosthesis was performed by Dr Hannes Jonker last week. Dr Jonker faced considerable pushback from fellow orthopaedic surgeons when he began questioning the traditional method, with many dismissing him as misguided. However, as scientific evidence emerged, it became clear that the key lies in achieving better balance. Studies indicate that kinematic alignment can provide significantly more balance—sometimes doubling that of mechanical alignment—resulting in less pain and improved long-term outcomes for patients. He explains in the video how the prosthesis is curved allowing the patella to move more freely around the knee joint.

Summary:
The amazing results are already being shown with our first case study: Mr Schalk Burger (not the rugby one). [The three patients who have already undergone surgery will be at Lenmed MooiMed Private Hospital in Potchefstroom for checkups on Aug 7th.]
One of the patients, Mr Schalk Burger, is a 58-year-old electrician (who goes up and down ladders all the time) from nearby Klerksdorp, Ottosdal, who has spent his life working on his knees. Before the surgery, he could barely walk due to severe pain in both knees, particularly his right knee, which was described as being bone-on-bone in his X-rays. He had to lean against objects for support and had a very low quality of life. Once an active individual who served in the army and played rugby, and was in agricultural college – all of which contributed to his knee problems. Burger found himself limited in movement, gained weight, and became depressed.
Now, just a week post-surgery, he is already walking pain-free and feels as though he’s 23 again! He can hardly believe the transformation. Although he will need surgery on his left knee in a few weeks, this procedure has given him a second chance at life.
Our other patient, Mr Andre Van Pletzen, is 56 years old and is a cinema, automation architect they make cinemas, and have a showroom in Kramerville, JHB... This job requires mobility, but Andre has struggled due to issues with his left knee. He can’t climb stairs, get on all fours, or perform daily tasks without difficulty. Van Pletzen is scheduled for surgery on August 7th, and we will be following his journey both before and after the procedure.


Further information:
We have secured a commitment for exclusivity from Dr Jonker, and his team has provided us with beautifully filmed footage of the first three surgeries. We will have access to all the raw footage, which will be invaluable for our project. Dr Jonker is also open to an intimate interview at his home on the afternoon of August 6th, which will give us deeper insights into his approach. Afterward, we’ll interview Van Pletzen at the hospital. Unfortunately, he won’t be available until then, as he will be at an expo for work. However, he is the only local patient among the three and will be checking in the night before the surgery.
The surgeries are scheduled for August 7th, from 7 AM to midday, followed by follow-up appointments with the patients. We have also secured permission to film inside the hospital, to film the surgeries and have reserved a room for conducting interviews.
Regarding the surgery and implant: this total knee arthroplasty procedure has been performed in Europe since October 2023. It aims to reconstruct patient-specific limb alignment and knee biomechanics based on the axis of the patient's femur, allowing for more natural knee movement. The implant is produced by the Swiss company Medacta SpheriKA, which specializes in kinematic alignment products. The doctor says, "Recovery is the same as with other types of replacements, it is the way the procedure is performed that differs and improves patient outcome and satisfaction. There is no additional cost to either the Medical Aid, patient or hospital. In an age where cost is a definite issue and the hype around robotic surgery incurs lots of cost on the medical system this is a great advantage.
Currently, there is no official register for total knee replacements in South Africa. However, according to Netcare hospitals, there are estimated to be between 8,000 and 10,000 knee replacements performed each year, with even more procedures conducted for hip replacements. This new approach has the potential to help thousands of patients in the coming years.

https://www.orthobullets.com/recon/423129/tka-kinematic-alignment
I’ve spoken with the doctor, and we have several exciting options to enhance our story. He has granted us access to Orthobullets, which features various slides and graphics that explain how the prosthesis works. While this is standard for similar stories and will provide valuable visual content, Chwayitisa suggested we aim for a more creative angle. The doctor is willing to demonstrate the differences in the operating theatre during the surgery, which adds a dynamic element.
I’d like the presenter to interact with the doctor during the procedure, and the entire crew will need to wear scrubs to fully immerse ourselves in the experience. We could even film the setup to capture that “Africa first” vibe. The main interview will take place in the theatre while standing, creating a more engaging atmosphere. Additionally, the doctor has invited us to his home the day before for a more personal interview, which will add depth to our story.
When considering what to show in the theatre, I found that the actual implementation of the implant may be too graphic for television, so we’ll need to explore options, dimming the colours in edit, using the graphics etc. We can display the implant outside of the body, and use a replica skeleton to explain its function. I suggest we present the explanations in three different ways to determine what resonates best with the presenter.
For the presenter links, I envision having the case studies in the background during the introductions. For example, we can show Mr. Van Pletzen struggling to climb stairs before his surgery while the presenter introduces him. And if Andre is up for it, we can show those first crucial steps after the surgery. Then, when introducing Mr. Burger, we could film him standing post-surgery, creating a compelling “miracle” moment that would work well on TV.
Additionally, when showcasing the prosthesis, we could zoom in on it and then fade into footage of the actual patient’s knee, helping to bring the experience to life for viewers. I saw this technique used effectively in another medical program, and I think it could enhance our storytelling.

Stay over in potch, and car rental

[Build expectation and tension]

Fade to Black

Govan: Is there an overarching philosophy behind kinematic alignment?
Dr Jonker: Yes. It's a technique that was brought out to try and place the knee in the same position where it was before it was diseased or in its arthritic position.
LINK: You might think when installing specifically in the hip, knee, and ankle, they need to be implanted in a straight line, that’s called mechanical alignment. (GRAPHIC showing straight line – hip knee and ankle)

Govan exercising…

LINK: Our bodies aren't perfectly symmetrical, Kinematic alignment is about implanting the prosthetic according to your body’s natural movement.

Govan: Why is kinematic alignment a breakthrough for knee replacements?
Dr Jonker: Because it respects the natural anatomy better. What I always tell the patients. I will not make your knee straight, I'm gonna make your knee the same way it was when you were 21 or 23 years old.

Dr Jonker: “There was a main line of thought, this is the way we were trained and this is the way you are supposed to put it in and that is the way that everyone should do it.

But Dr Jonker saw room for improvement.

Dr Jonker: literature shows you that almost 19 or 20% of patients that have knee replacement surgery are not happy with their results, that's a very high percentage

VO: Studies show that in comparison to mechanical alignment, Kinematic alignment increases surgical success by promoting better recovery and can be applied to other joint surgeries.

Dr Jonker: When I started out there wasn't much literatures to support what I was believing Over the last 4, 5 years numerous publications has been released that shows the benefits in patient satisfaction and that is potentially outperforming the mechanical alignments

VO: Swiss medical prosthetics company Medacta released the SpheriKA implant in late 2023. It's groundbreaking as the first and only prosthesis specifically designed around this innovative philosophy. This groove is wider than the one in a traditional implant, which means it fits a variety of natural knee shapes more comfortably.

Dr Jonker: The prosthesis that we put in moves, and the combination with this specific prosthesis with the kinematic aligned knee mimics the way the normal knee moves or the natural knee moves the best

VO: Dr Jonker predicts this technique will become the standard for knee replacements, starting with patients who have severe joint damage and won't benefit from traditional methods.

VO: 58 year old Schalk Burger was one of these… He injured both his knees twenty years ago, bringing his lifestyle to a halt…

Since then, the mine manager has lived in constant pain barely able to walk.

Schalk: It was painful walking down to the plant where I used to walk three times a day. I started limiting time in the plant to maybe once a day.

X-rays show his cartilage in his right knee has virtually gone, making it hard to enjoy time with his wife Analie.

Schalk interview: it's about quality of life with my wife, with my kids, interaction with my family. You know simple thing is going to a mall with your wife.

In late July, he was the first patient in Africa to receive the SpheriKA implant. After his surgery, we joined him for a check-up. at Mooimed Hospital.

Dr Jonker: You happy with the swelling, his performance he's doing very very well yeah he'll be probably be ready to start driving his car….


VO: But will doctor Jonker’s next operation be as successful? We’ll join 56- year-old Andre van Pletzen as he undergoes this pioneering surgery. He believes it's his best chance to walk normally again. [create tension]

Govan: what are your expectations?
Andre: I hope it's good it's gonna work out well you know
Govan: they say they they return the knee to its status that it was when you were 21 years old
Govan: Hope so!
Years of wear and tear have worn away his cartilage leaving the automation technician with a noticeable limp.
show

Andre: You can't really walk. It’s sore, you have to stand around a little bit to get it going again.

And these days, walking up and down stairs is a challenge… show…

Govan: For your kind of job do you have to get down on all fours and crawl under stuff?
Andre: Yes, it's not too bad to get down, just to get up again, it's quite a mission because you can't bend your leg.

FADE TO BLACK (outside hospital shot)

Govan gets ready, and says a link outside hospital room:
In a few moments…

The procedure takes only 45 minutes… upsounds

Govan: Doc, what are you what are you doing there?
Dr Jonker: I'm aligning the knee right

nats sound

See Dr showing the prosthesis and putting it in…

Operation 5 clips: Govan: We can't show you guys much of what's happening here because well it's Sunday night and it's not necessarily what you want to see while you're having your second plate of food.

VO: But we’ll show the highlights. The damaged cartilage is removed from the patient to make room for the implant.

Dr Jonker: That's the so so what you can see there, it's bone on bone on that side.

Govan: They're getting into a crucial stage of the operation

[see dr jonker putting silver joint in knee.]

VO: And just like that Andre has a new knee…

See Dr Jonker move the knee up and down …

VO: It’s now a waiting game as the patient heals – which takes roughly six months.

Schalk has already started his physio and recovery exercises.

Govan in waiting room…LINK 5980: There is no additional cost for the medical aid, the patient or the hospital, and as we know that cost is always a significant concern, this presents a considerable advantage.

VO: Just a few hours after his surgery, Andre took his first steps toward recovery—steps that could greatly improve his chances of living a normal life again.

VO: So why is kinematic alignment so life changing - well, Schalk shows us as he surprises everyone – even me – by already starting to walk… (capture moment)

Dr Jonker: And this is where the satisfaction comes in, you know, someone that couldn't walk before, improving his quality of life.
Govan: Must be nice being in control again?
Schalk: I didn't want to walk, I couldn't, it was too sore, I walked 20, 30 steps and then I sat down and walked another 20, 30 steps.
Govan: oh no man and now?
Schalk: Well I can walk.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A groundbreaking new technique for knee replacement has been performed in an African-first surgery right here in Johannesburg, led by renowned surgeon Dr. Hannes Jonker.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: You might assume that when replacing body parts with implants, they should be aligned in a straight line—specifically in alignment with the hip, knee, and ankle (HKA alignment, both from the front and the side). This approach, known as mechanical alignment, has been the traditional method for implanting knee replacement prostheses. The idea was that this alignment would reduce stress on the knee, promoting the long-term durability of the implant. However, our bodies aren’t perfectly designed; individuals often have anatomical variations in their knees and surrounding ligaments due to normal wear and tear. Since 2019, the perspective on prosthesis implantation has shifted to a new philosophy called kinematic alignment, which has shown significantly better outcomes. This approach aligns the prosthetic with your body’s natural or native alignment—essentially reflecting how your body functioned when you were in your 20s and pre-arthritic. Kinematic alignment is a fresh perspective on implants and has been applied to other types of prosthetics, such as hip replacements. What is different in this ‘Africa first’ surgery is that it’s the first time an actual implant has been specifically designed and implemented (the SpheriKA prosthesis) around this innovative philosophy. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGuGJSxpLoE “Kinematic Alignment (KA) is a technique designed to restore the knee to its pre-arthritic anatomical alignment. It focuses on customising replacement components to a patient’s unique anatomy, biomechanics and motion patterns, aiming to achieve more natural knee movement, better functional outcomes, improved range of motion and greater implant durability.” The first surgery in Africa using this prosthesis was performed by Dr Hannes Jonker last week. Dr Jonker faced considerable pushback from fellow orthopaedic surgeons when he began questioning the traditional method, with many dismissing him as misguided. However, as scientific evidence emerged, it became clear that the key lies in achieving better balance. Studies indicate that kinematic alignment can provide significantly more balance—sometimes doubling that of mechanical alignment—resulting in less pain and improved long-term outcomes for patients. He explains in the video how the prosthesis is curved allowing the patella to move more freely around the knee joint.
metadata.Summary: The amazing results are already being shown with our first case study: Mr Schalk Burger (not the rugby one). [The three patients who have already undergone surgery will be at Lenmed MooiMed Private Hospital in Potchefstroom for checkups on Aug 7th.] One of the patients, Mr Schalk Burger, is a 58-year-old electrician (who goes up and down ladders all the time) from nearby Klerksdorp, Ottosdal, who has spent his life working on his knees. Before the surgery, he could barely walk due to severe pain in both knees, particularly his right knee, which was described as being bone-on-bone in his X-rays. He had to lean against objects for support and had a very low quality of life. Once an active individual who served in the army and played rugby, and was in agricultural college – all of which contributed to his knee problems. Burger found himself limited in movement, gained weight, and became depressed. Now, just a week post-surgery, he is already walking pain-free and feels as though he’s 23 again! He can hardly believe the transformation. Although he will need surgery on his left knee in a few weeks, this procedure has given him a second chance at life. Our other patient, Mr Andre Van Pletzen, is 56 years old and is a cinema, automation architect they make cinemas, and have a showroom in Kramerville, JHB... This job requires mobility, but Andre has struggled due to issues with his left knee. He can’t climb stairs, get on all fours, or perform daily tasks without difficulty. Van Pletzen is scheduled for surgery on August 7th, and we will be following his journey both before and after the procedure.
metadata.Further information: We have secured a commitment for exclusivity from Dr Jonker, and his team has provided us with beautifully filmed footage of the first three surgeries. We will have access to all the raw footage, which will be invaluable for our project. Dr Jonker is also open to an intimate interview at his home on the afternoon of August 6th, which will give us deeper insights into his approach. Afterward, we’ll interview Van Pletzen at the hospital. Unfortunately, he won’t be available until then, as he will be at an expo for work. However, he is the only local patient among the three and will be checking in the night before the surgery. The surgeries are scheduled for August 7th, from 7 AM to midday, followed by follow-up appointments with the patients. We have also secured permission to film inside the hospital, to film the surgeries and have reserved a room for conducting interviews. Regarding the surgery and implant: this total knee arthroplasty procedure has been performed in Europe since October 2023. It aims to reconstruct patient-specific limb alignment and knee biomechanics based on the axis of the patient's femur, allowing for more natural knee movement. The implant is produced by the Swiss company Medacta SpheriKA, which specializes in kinematic alignment products. The doctor says, "Recovery is the same as with other types of replacements, it is the way the procedure is performed that differs and improves patient outcome and satisfaction. There is no additional cost to either the Medical Aid, patient or hospital. In an age where cost is a definite issue and the hype around robotic surgery incurs lots of cost on the medical system this is a great advantage. Currently, there is no official register for total knee replacements in South Africa. However, according to Netcare hospitals, there are estimated to be between 8,000 and 10,000 knee replacements performed each year, with even more procedures conducted for hip replacements. This new approach has the potential to help thousands of patients in the coming years. https://www.orthobullets.com/recon/423129/tka-kinematic-alignment I’ve spoken with the doctor, and we have several exciting options to enhance our story. He has granted us access to Orthobullets, which features various slides and graphics that explain how the prosthesis works. While this is standard for similar stories and will provide valuable visual content, Chwayitisa suggested we aim for a more creative angle. The doctor is willing to demonstrate the differences in the operating theatre during the surgery, which adds a dynamic element. I’d like the presenter to interact with the doctor during the procedure, and the entire crew will need to wear scrubs to fully immerse ourselves in the experience. We could even film the setup to capture that “Africa first” vibe. The main interview will take place in the theatre while standing, creating a more engaging atmosphere. Additionally, the doctor has invited us to his home the day before for a more personal interview, which will add depth to our story. When considering what to show in the theatre, I found that the actual implementation of the implant may be too graphic for television, so we’ll need to explore options, dimming the colours in edit, using the graphics etc. We can display the implant outside of the body, and use a replica skeleton to explain its function. I suggest we present the explanations in three different ways to determine what resonates best with the presenter. For the presenter links, I envision having the case studies in the background during the introductions. For example, we can show Mr. Van Pletzen struggling to climb stairs before his surgery while the presenter introduces him. And if Andre is up for it, we can show those first crucial steps after the surgery. Then, when introducing Mr. Burger, we could film him standing post-surgery, creating a compelling “miracle” moment that would work well on TV. Additionally, when showcasing the prosthesis, we could zoom in on it and then fade into footage of the actual patient’s knee, helping to bring the experience to life for viewers. I saw this technique used effectively in another medical program, and I think it could enhance our storytelling.
